dogmatic

/dog-MAT-ik/ - the stress falls on MAT · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dogmatic means asserting unproved principles as unquestionable truth — aggressively and arrogantly certain about beliefs no one is allowed to examine.

Coach Benítez is dogmatic about the 4-4-2: formations that win championships elsewhere are, to him, heresies not worth discussing.

Example

Over thirty years on the forum, the astronomy club's founder grew dogmatic: any photograph that contradicted his pet theory was waved off as 'amateur error,' and when new members asked what evidence supported the theory itself, he replied that some things are simply understood.

Notice what's missing: proof, and any willingness to be questioned. He doesn't argue for his belief — he hands it down as settled truth and treats the question itself as the offense. That arrogant certainty about an unproved principle is exactly what dogmatic condemns.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

doctrinaire: Doctrinaire means determined to apply a pet theory to every situation, workable or not — it's about forcing the doctrine into practice. Dogmatic is about the manner of belief itself: laying down unproved principles as truths no one may question.

inflexible: Inflexible means unwilling to bend — about plans, rules, or schedules of any kind. Dogmatic is inflexibility about beliefs specifically, delivered with the arrogance of total certainty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

open-minded: willing to weigh ideas that challenge your own

receptive: ready to take in new evidence and arguments

Where it sits · how completely the mind has closed

opinionated → dogmatic → fanatical

opinionated vs. dogmatic: Opinionated is weaker than dogmatic: an opinionated uncle has strong views on everything and enjoys the argument, while a dogmatic one hands his views down as settled truths no argument may touch.

fanatical vs. dogmatic: Fanatical is stronger than dogmatic: the dogmatic mind still bothers to declare its unproved certainties, while the fanatical one has fused with them — beyond question, beyond proportion, sometimes beyond reason entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dogmat-: an opinion laid down as true (Greek dogma, from dokein, 'to think, to seem true')

Suffix — -ic: having the character of

Put it together: Dogma (Greek, 'an opinion laid down as true' — from dokein, 'to think, to seem') + -ic = having the character of a dogma. The word carries its history: a dogmatic speaker treats mere opinion as official doctrine, proclaimed rather than proved.

Use the root in a new word: orthodox: Nothing about the quartet's phrasing is orthodox, and the critics cannot decide whether that delights or alarms them.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical

Dogmatic condemns the manner, not the belief: a person can be right and still dogmatic if they proclaim rather than prove. Confident and firm can be compliments; dogmatic never is — it adds arrogance and the refusal to be questioned. Its parent noun dogma stays neutral in religion, where it names official doctrine, but turns pejorative almost everywhere else.
